claims.text: WTaTiVZr is an equimolar five-element alloy.
WTaTiVZr has a multi-principal-element BCC matrix.
The WTaTiVZr constituent elements are relatively low-activation or reduced-activity metals.
Atomic-size mismatch and chemical complexity produce significant local lattice distortion in WTaTiVZr.
The local complexity of WTaTiVZr facilitates diverse slip pathways.
Plastic deformation in WTaTiVZr involves substantial dislocation activity.
Lattice distortion slows and redistributes dislocation motion in WTaTiVZr.
Redistributed dislocation motion increases WTaTiVZr's capacity for plastic deformation.
Enhanced dislocation activity and lattice distortion delay crack initiation and propagation through crack-tip blunting.
At 800–1200 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater tensile elongation than pure tungsten under matched test conditions.
At 800–1200 °C, WTaTiVZr will exhibit greater fracture toughness than pure tungsten under matched test conditions.
WTaTiVZr will display more uniform plastic flow before failure than pure tungsten.
Pure tungsten has very limited plastic strain and high brittleness under the proposed high-temperature mechanical loading.
Matching fabrication route and grain size between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten is intended to isolate alloy composition as the comparison variable.
The comparison will use tensile and fracture-toughness tests at 800–1200 °C with identical strain rates and thermal profiles in inert gas or vacuum.
Large departures from equimolar composition or formation of detrimental intermetallic phases may eliminate the proposed ductility and toughness improvements.
Extended service or temperatures outside the tested range may alter the beneficial structural features of WTaTiVZr.
Prior refractory high-entropy-alloy studies suggest improved deformation capacity, but do not establish the proposed WTaTiVZr-versus-tungsten toughness advantage.
